payload.description:
## Trigger
The Anthropic prompting audit (2026-09-12) read `.claude/output-styles/tired-engineer.md` and found the rule "Report status often. Report before a wait over 1 minute, and after every third tool call."

## Problem
A model cannot count its own tool calls reliably, so the rule is either ignored or obeyed as scaffolding: a status block appears on a cadence rather than when the reader needs one. A cadence rule spends output on nothing when three calls change nothing, and stays silent when one call changes everything.

## Fix
State the condition that makes a report useful instead of a count. Report when the plan changes, when a step fails, when a wait will exceed a minute, and when the reader must decide.

## Acceptance
- No numeric tool-call cadence remains in the style.
- The replacement names conditions the model can observe.

## Scope
- `.claude/output-styles/tired-engineer.md`

payload.description:
## Context

D26 is explicit: **a dispatch with no resolved tier is a bug, not a default** - an omitted model inherits the session's, which is usually the most expensive one, so the routing rule defeats itself silently.

Found while running the admission test for a new role, 2026-08-14.

## Measured

- agent.schema.json required is [schema_version, name, purpose, triggers, returns, posture, tools, slots]. **tier is optional.**
- code-reviewer and security-auditor declare no tier. agents.py:307 reads str(data.get('tier') or '').strip(), so both resolve to the empty string.
- basicly catalog lint and basicly agents-check both pass on that tree, so no gate binds.
- Both are ad-hoc agents vendored to consumers by basicly install, so a consumer inherits the untier-ed pair.
- Nobody declares maximum at all. The ladder has four rungs and the roster uses three, which is the same dead-definition shape recorded for skills.

## What the fix is

Make tier required in the schema, assign one to the two roles that lack it, and let catalog lint refuse a source without it. Assigning the tiers is a judgement per role and is the part that needs a human.

## Relationship to basicly-a3yi

Different halves of the same rule and both are needed. a3yi resolves a **declared** tier into the projected surface that has a model slot. This bead is that a tier can be **undeclared** and nothing notices - so a3yi could land in full and these two roles would still spawn on whatever the session is running.

## Note on the third half

Verified 2026-08-14: the tier kit ships (.basicly/core/kit/tier/claude_tier_hook.py) and its hook is **not installed in this repo** - .claude/settings.json registers PreToolUse and PostToolUse only. So a declared tier reaches no spawn here today, by any path.
payload.title: the agent schema lets a role ship with no tier and two already do

payload.description:
## Context

Owner request 2026-08-22: *"run this analysis using fable 5 (tier max) so I can actually see lanes on the board with different models at the same time, as that is also a use case."*

Neither half is reachable today.

## Measured

**A tier cannot be chosen for a run.** `loop supervise` takes `--runner` and `--autonomy` and nothing else. Both are applied through `session.set_override`, a process-scoped registry whose whole purpose is *"configuring a run is deterministic, so it should be one command rather than a config edit plus a revert the operator has to remember"*. `[runner] default_tier = "high"` is committed config, so selecting `maximum` today means editing `basicly.toml`, which that module's own docstring names as the wrong answer: it *"changes behaviour for every consumer"*.

`maximum` resolves to `claude-fable-5` on anthropic, per `.basicly/core/models/model-map.json`.

**Two models cannot appear on one board.** `runner.select_runner` is called once per round, at `supervise.py:1457` and `supervise.py:2010`, and its result is the spec for every lane in that pass. There is no per-lane resolution; `basicly-a3yi` is the record for that and is unbuilt.

## What this record does, and what it does not

It adds `--tier` to `loop supervise`, wired exactly as `--autonomy` is: validated against the known tiers, applied through `session.set_override("runner", "default_tier", ...)`, and recorded in every run record for free because `run_record` already writes `session.override_pairs()`.

It does **not** add per-lane tiers. That stays `basicly-a3yi`.

## Why one model per pass still gives two on the board

`basicly-0hxck3` landed the lane card reading `model` from each lane's **own last run record**, not from the pass's spec. So a lane whose previous dispatch ran on `claude-opus-5` renders `claude-opus-5` while a lane dispatched now on `claude-fable-5` renders `claude-fable-5`. Two models on one board follows from per-lane provenance, without per-lane selection - and that is worth stating because it is the difference between the board *reporting* a mixed fleet and the engine *dispatching* one.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `uv run basicly loop supervise --help`
2. Look for a flag that selects a model tier.

**Observed.** `--label`, `--max-passes`, `--runner`, `--autonomy`. No tier flag.

**Control.** `--autonomy` is present and does the same kind of thing through the same registry, so the mechanism exists and only this key is unreachable. And `grep default_tier basicly.toml` returns `default_tier = "high"`, so the key is real and committed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN an operator names a tier for one run, THE DISPATCH SHALL use it and NO COMMITTED FILE SHALL change.
- WHEN a tier is named that is not a known tier, THE COMMAND SHALL refuse before applying any override, on the same all-or-nothing rule `--runner` and `--autonomy` already follow.
- WHEN a tier override is active, THE RUN RECORD SHALL carry it, and the session header SHALL print it, because a session not running on committed config must say so.
- WHEN no tier is named, THE BEHAVIOUR SHALL be unchanged and the committed default SHALL apply.
- WHERE a tier resolves to no available model for the chosen surface, THE DISPATCH SHALL refuse rather than fall back to a neighbouring tier, which is the rule the model map states for itself.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_session_overrides.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `60000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Run `loop supervise --tier maximum` and read `claude-fable-5` in the dispatch line and in the run record, against a control run with no flag that reads `claude-opus-5`, and a third with a bogus tier that refuses before overriding anything.

Landed by hand on main 2026-08-22 and verified there. loop supervise now takes --tier {low,medium,high,maximum}, applied through the same session-override registry as --runner and --autonomy, validated before anything is applied, and recorded in every run record because build_record stamps the override pairs centrally.

Proved end to end rather than at the parser: with no flag the loaded spec carries tier high and resolves through the model map to claude-opus-5; with --tier maximum it carries maximum and resolves to claude-fable-5. Removing the branch kills exactly the three tests that assert it and nothing else. uv run basicly verify --mode full is PASS on main after the merge.

Hand-landed rather than looped because the flag had to be on main before a supervised pass could use it, and the pass is what was asked for. One commit, merge-tested clean first.

cli.py is rebaselined by the 266 tokens the flag costs, with a reason and a base commit, rather than waived - a waiver replaces a frozen entry outright and would have deleted its 54336-token ceiling to buy 266 tokens. That is the first use of the rebaseline route since the guidance describing it was corrected under basicly-03ykuf, and the guidance was missing one detail the gate then named: base_commit belongs in [ratchet], not in [ratchet.<gate>].

Per-lane tiers are NOT this record and remain basicly-a3yi: select_runner resolves one spec a round.

payload.text:
[claim corrected 2026-08-22, owner challenged it and was right] This record's context said a run could not choose a model tier and that fable-5 was unreachable without a config edit. The second half is literally true and the first is wrong, and the framing turned an existing capability into a missing one.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTED, proved on a scratch config with no code change:

  claude-max   tier=maximum  source=agent tier -> claude-fable-5
  claude-mid   tier=medium   source=agent tier -> claude-sonnet-5

A [[runner.agents]] entry takes tier and vendor. It is documented at config.py:190-197, parsed by _parse_model_tier at config.py:1716, recorded as tier_source AGENT_TIER, and resolved through .basicly/core/models/model-map.json by models.model_for. Declaring an agent with tier maximum and passing --runner claude-max would have dispatched fable-5 today.

AND TWO MODELS AT ONCE ALREADY WORKED, which is the part I got most wrong:

  lanes    -> agent=claude-max   tier=maximum  model=claude-fable-5
  decider  -> agent=claude-mid   tier=medium   model=claude-sonnet-5

[runner] decider selects a different agent for decider invocations - loop.py:1142 and decisions.py:387 resolve config.decider or config.default. So a per-ROLE model split shipped long ago.

SO WHAT IS THIS FLAG WORTH. It saves a config edit for a one-off run, which is the session-override registry's stated purpose, and it is recorded in the run record. That is a convenience and it is worth having. It is NOT an enabling change and the record should not have read as one.

WHAT REMAINS GENUINELY ABSENT, unchanged: two lanes in the same lane set cannot run different models, because supervise.py:2010 resolves one spec and dispatches every admitted lane with it. That is basicly-a3yi.

WHY I MISSED IT: [runner] decider is read at config.py:1627 and appears nowhere in basicly.toml - four grep hits, all prose about the decider's corpus, none a key or an example - while default, max_agent_processes and the whole [[runner.agents]] block are documented in that same file. Filed as basicly-rrnthf. The lesson is mine though: I read the config file and the argparse surface and stopped, when the loader is the authority on what a section accepts.

## The defect

The producer validates the in-memory payload, the transport truncates it, and the consumer re-reads the stored body and refuses it. The producing function's own docstring claims it is validated before the write so a producing state can never hand on an artifact the consuming state will refuse. That sentence is false.

Measured over the committed ledger 2026-08-18: 31 of 54 handoff artifacts are cut, 337353 bytes lost. **23 record and kind pairs are refused by their own entry predicate and the bodies are unrecoverable**, because the external binary is deleted and the log may not be rewritten. 20 of 21 artifacts written live by the engine were truncated, so this is not an import artefact.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Call the entry predicate for the implementation-plan of `basicly-ejdm`.
2. Call it for the change-summary of `basicly-0p8n` as a positive control.
3. Scan the ledger for artifact markers and compare their stored length against their recorded original length.

Observed: step 1 returns not admitted, with a reason quoting JSON cut mid-token. Step 2 returns admitted. `basicly-ejdm` is open and in decompose.
Expected: a body the producer validated is the body the consumer reads.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given a producing state records an artifact then the engine appends one `artifact` event carrying the kind as a typed field and the body under a non-truncatable key.
Given the stored body is read back by the entry predicate then it is byte-identical to what the producer validated.
Given a legacy artifact marker on disk then the reader resolves it to the `artifact` kind through the delegated-kind alias rather than the skip path.
Given a repository that has not installed the schemas then neither end runs.
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_artifact_record.py tests/test_handoff.py -q, plus recording a 20000-byte artifact and asserting the entry predicate admits it, which is red today against 23 real pairs

## Also fixes

Two module docstrings assert the external tracker mode as a live fact. Both are defects under the comment-divergence decision.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/artifact_record.py`
- `src/basicly/handoff.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `tests/test_artifact_record.py`
- `tests/test_handoff.py`

payload.description:
# Multi-project tracker architecture: session of 2026-11-11

Owner request 2026-11-11: hill-climb, agent swarm and council to find the best long-lived architecture for a work tracker that serves many registered projects, outlives the code repositories, is configurable, and never lets a project forget to update it, so every team member knows who works on what and the progress. Novel solutions allowed. The agents were to find the requirements the owner forgot.

## Status at stop

- Done: requirements discovery swarm (6 Opus lenses), 5 independent Opus architectures, verification of key claims (3 fresh Opus agents, 2 with measurements), council (5 blind Opus voters), hill-climb round 1 (5 Opus graders plus a verifier).
- Council decision, 5 of 5: git-budget. All shared state in ordinary git repositories on GitHub or Bitbucket, no server. A registry repository; one vault (backlog) repository per project; one append-only file set per writer machine; claims push at once with compare-and-swap; other events batched under a push budget. Every voter named the same counter-argument: N4 "shared in time" is undefined; comments arrive after 2 to 4 minutes.
- Hill-climb round 1 on design version 8 (v1): grades fit-to-need 4-6, longevity 4-7, simplicity 5-6, poka-yoke 3-6, operability 3-6, testability 2-6, recovery 2-7; 53 important findings; a verifier refuted 0 of the 12 most important. The script decided: continue.
- In progress at stop: the author was revising to v2 from the round-1 findings. Round-2 lenses planned: architecture, poka-yoke, recovery, tests, security, simplicity.
- Next: finish the climb (rounds 2 to at most 5), then present the final design and the open owner decisions. No code before owner approval. S1 (git_runner.py) is built and closed; S2 to S4 of v7 are on hold until this design is decided, because v8 changes S2 and S3.

## Open owner decisions (recommendations from the author of v8)

1. N4 in seconds: recommended claims answered within 10 s at p99; other events shared within about 4 minutes at 13 machines, with freshness shown on every view.
2. Identity binding to host accounts: recommended to stay deferred.
3. Erasure of personal data under append-only history: recommended not built; it would be an announced history rewrite.
4. Forecast: recommended to drop "estimate" from the SPEC non-goal (SPEC.md:741), because the board must answer "when will the work be done".
5. Commit hook refuses a commit with no record id and fills it when the session holds exactly one claim (reverses v7).
6. Bitbucket Free holds about one project of 1M events (measured 0.5 to 0.7 KB per stored event at best).


## Verification results


## verify-service (falsify-first on arch/service-mirror.md): fail, all five claims break as written

- C1 "a lost service loses at most one 15 s batch of order, never data": refuted. A forge outage lets the service's write-ahead log grow past one batch; a disk loss then loses the order of the whole outage, and the events of clients that already exited. A restart at the same URL after a wiped disk reuses (epoch, seq) numbers. Void verdicts are not published, so voided events are re-sent forever.
- C2 "a changed claim is bounded to 15 s and always reported": refuted. An old service cut off from the forge never sees the failover fence; a holder whose session ended is never told; /clear changes the session id; a plain crash has no report path.
- C3 "direct mode and service mode fold to the same records": refuted. An offline direct-mode writer that pushes after a switch is voided as foreign and also dropped; service write-time checks have no fold-time twin.
- C4 "meets C3 and idiot-proof for a team with no server": partly. No stated path to choose direct mode; OPEN.md missing or stale in direct mode; N3 and N4 weaker in direct mode.
- C5 "SSH signing works without a prompt on three platforms": refuted on Linux alone (OpenSSH 10.2p1: a passphrase key without an agent calls askpass and exits 255; file mode prompts "Overwrite (y/n)?"). Windows and macOS not measured.
- Fixes named by the verifier: epoch bump on every start, a bound on unpublished events, publish void verdicts, a claim lease tied to the last publish, every check run at fold time in both modes, sign only through the agent with SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=never.

## verify-storage (measured on local bare repositories): fail

- Measured 100,000 synthetic events built from real ledger lines (about 1.4 KB raw each), 50 writers, log/<year>/<writer>.jsonl, 5 to 20 events per commit.
- Stored size per event: 463 B with gc --aggressive, 640 B with a normal repack; with deep history per file (2 writers, 20k events) 668 B aggressive and 3.3 KB with a normal repack. A shallow clone of the current files alone: 424 B per event.
- Clone time of the 100k repository: 1.5 s locally.
- A regenerated summary file (OPEN.md) rewritten on each commit adds 0.8 to 1.9 KB per commit.
- Claim "about 300 B per event, 1M events about 300 MB": refuted (300 B is a zlib figure with no history).
- Claim "1M events under 100 MB": refuted (the current files alone need about 300 to 420 MB).
- Claim "1M events under Bitbucket Free's 1 GB": partly; only with aggressive repacking, which the host controls, not the tool.
- Consequence: growing per-writer files rewritten per commit cost history per version. Designs should append into small files (rotate monthly or by size), never rewrite a whole growing file, and drop summary files from commits. A 1M-event project is about 0.5 to 0.7 GB at best; Bitbucket Free (1 GB per workspace) holds about one such project.

## verify-contention (simulation on local bare repositories, 13 machines x 4 sessions = 52 writers): partly confirmed

- Setup: push latency 1.5 s (pre-receive sleep), fetch 0.5 s; compare-and-swap share with plumbing; claims 1 per session per 20 min; 10 other events per session per hour; 40 simulated minutes, 6 replicas of the budget policy (A) and 2 of push-every-event (B); time scaled 2x, checked at 1x.

| | A: claims at once, others batched | B: every event pushes |
|---|---|---|
| Attempted pushes per minute, mean | 5.06 | 17.19 |
| Busiest 60 s, attempted | 12 to 18 | 46 to 58 |
| Claim p50 / p95 / p99 / max | 2.1 / 4.2 / 6.3 / 8.3 s | 2.1 / 8.3 / 12.0 / 16.6 s |
| Claims over 10 s | 0 of 651 | 5 of 223 |
| Non-claim visibility p50 / p95 | 109 / 218 s | 2.1 / 6.3 s |

- Burst: 13 claims in the same second; the k-th winner answers after about 2k seconds; 9 of 13 over 10 s; max 26.5 s; 91 push attempts for 13 wins.
- Verdict: steady state at about 50 writers meets "about 6 pushes per minute on average and claim p99 within 10 s". It fails for the busiest minute (12 to 18 attempts) and for 5 or more simultaneous claims. The budget does not limit claim pushes; at one claim per session every 8 minutes claims alone reach 6 per minute (arithmetic, not measured). Comments and fields become visible after about 2 to 4 minutes.

## Requirements found by the swarm and verified vendor facts (requirements version 1, sections 6 and 7)

## 6. Requirements found by the discovery swarm (2026-11-11, 6 Opus lenses, not yet confirmed by the owner)

Each line is a "shall" requirement in short form. The lens that found it is in brackets. "Owner call" marks a line that conflicts with an earlier owner decision or a SPEC non-goal; the architecture must not make it impossible, but it is not built until the owner decides.

### 6.1 Projects and identity of data
- P1 One non-interactive, repeatable command registers a project; a duplicate prefix or code URL is refused by name; a list command shows every project. [adoption]
- P2 A project has a permanent identity independent of its repository name, URL or host; the code location is a changeable attribute with history; a project can be archived read-only and restored. [longevity]
- P3 Record ids are unique across all projects of one tracker and never reused; each prefix has one owning project; old prefixes resolve as aliases after a rename. [longevity]
- P4 The backlog moves between GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab and a plain bare git repository with no change to any record or id; no host identifier is used as identity. [longevity]
- P5 Configuration changes (rename or remove a status, field or workflow) never make old records unreadable or change the meaning of recorded events. [longevity]

### 6.2 Visibility for a lead (the "everyone knows who works on what" goal)
- V1 One portfolio view (command and board) lists every project: in progress with holders, blocked, stale claims, ready count, closed in the last 7 days, forecast. [team-lead]
- V2 A claim with no holder activity for a configurable time is flagged stale with holder and age; it is never released automatically; one command takes it and names the old holder. [team-lead, workflow]
- V3 A list of misses per project: merged default-branch changes that name no record, in-progress records with no code activity, unconfirmed suggestions, each with age. [team-lead]
- V4 Commit or pull request work by a holder with no claim is reported at the next commit, session start or tracker command, with the exact claim command. [workflow]
- V5 Every view shows, per project and writer, the time of the last shared event and any unshared local events (freshness). [team-lead]
- V6 Forecast of a completion range from measured throughput, with confidence and sample size. Owner call: contradicts the SPEC.md:741 non-goal "no estimate or reporting ceremony". [team-lead]
- V7 (nit) Handover event; time in status; changes since a date; subscribe to notices without polling; linked branch, pull request and last commit per in-progress record. [team-lead, workflow]

### 6.3 Developers and agents
- D1 Same state from any worktree, subdirectory or branch on one machine; a write is visible to a read in another worktree before the write returns. [workflow]
- D2 A holder can hand claims to another session or person; a restarted session (after /clear, resume, compaction) can take back its own claims with one logged command. [workflow]
- D3 Each session of Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and a person gets its own holder identity automatically. [workflow]
- D4 Every event records actor kind (person or agent session) and, for an agent, the responsible person who launched it. [team-lead]
- D5 Machine-readable output with a versioned schema; documented exit codes for success, refusal, held, pending, offline and internal error; stable within a major version. [workflow]
- D6 Offline: every read works from the last fetched state and prints its age; comments, notes and non-claim changes queue and share later exactly once. [workflow]
- D7 No command prompts, opens an editor or a pager; every refusal names its cause and one exact next command, with no traceback. [workflow, adoption]

### 6.4 Scale and speed (numbers proposed by the scale lens; owner may change them)
- S1 At least 50000 records and 1000000 events per project; store under 1 GB and under 1000 files after 5 years, including per-writer files. [scale]
- S2 On 4 cores with 10000 records: read p95 at most 1 s, local append p95 at most 200 ms, independent of the network. [scale]
- S3 At least 50 concurrent writers per project, 16 agent sessions on one 4-core machine, no lost or duplicated event. [scale]
- S4 With 50 writers and 1 to 2 s latency on real GitHub and Bitbucket: 99% of claims answered within 10 s, none unclear after 60 s. [scale]
- S5 Stay within published forge limits (GitHub push and fetch rate guidance, Bitbucket size limits) at peak load; no throttling. [scale] (facts under verification)
- S6 A shared change is visible to every online writer within 60 s at p95 without a manual command. [scale]
- S7 Under slow or flaky networks no command exceeds its deadline; queued events share within 5 minutes after the network returns. [scale]
- S8 (nit) 100 projects per machine; board first view within 2 s; a 5-year clone within 60 s at 10 Mbit/s. [scale]

### 6.5 Security, access and privacy
- X1 Per-project read isolation: no title, comment, id or dependency endpoint of a project reaches someone without read access; a backlog more visible than its code repository is refused. [security]
- X2 Events are attributable to an authenticated host identity; an event whose writer id does not match the pusher is void and reported. Owner call: conflicts with deferral (b) of identity binding. [security]
- X3 Any change to another writer's data, and any removal or rewrite of shared events, is detected and reported at the next command of every clone. [security]
- X4 Redaction of secrets and absolute paths is on by default on every write path, including the standalone CLI. [security]
- X5 Erasure of a named person's personal data from every copy with a pseudonymous audit stub. Owner call: in tension with append-only history. [security]
- X6 Record text is untrusted data for agents: marked by a fixed delimiter; no command runs, fetches or follows record text. [security]
- X7 Only the user's existing git credentials or a credential store; no token written anywhere by the tracker; a CI token is limited to one backlog repository. [security]
- X8 The board accepts state changes only from its own page (per-session token, Host and Origin checks) and binds only to loopback. [security]
- X9 (nit) Roles per project for close, take, descope, delete, configure; complete audit trail of who, when, command, session. [security]

### 6.6 Longevity
- L1 Every stored event carries a format version; every release reads every earlier format, with no time limit. [longevity]
- L2 Lossless export of a whole backlog to a documented plain-text format; a reader written from the spec alone rebuilds the records. [longevity]
- L3 A stated 10-year growth budget; with 10 years of synthetic history (100000 records) fold and clone stay within limits. [longevity]
- L4 Restore onto a new host from any clone or export, with an integrity check and a stated recovery point. [longevity]
- L5 Commit links survive rebase, squash, deleted branch or deleted repository, or are reported as unreachable. [longevity]
- L6 (nit) UTC RFC 3339 timestamps. [longevity]

### 6.7 Adoption, upgrade, removal
- A1 Two tool versions writing one backlog lose no event and block no writer; an old version reads what it can or refuses by name with the upgrade command. [adoption]
- A2 One upgrade command upgrades tool and data format, prints versions, resumes after a crash, refuses a downgrade by name. [adoption]
- A3 A new member on a new machine reaches a first claim from one README line; each missing piece (tool, clone, host access, hook) is refused with the exact next command. [adoption]
- A4 One explicit removal command per project and per machine deletes everything install wrote, exports data first and reports leftovers. [adoption]
- A5 Lossless, repeatable, previewable migration from beads, beans and the in-repository ledger, verified by count and digest. [adoption]
- A6 Install, attach, claim, serve and removal pass on Linux, macOS and Windows, including paths with spaces. [adoption]
- A7 (nit) A doctor command; README install pins checked by a gate. [adoption]

- GitHub: "Push rate: The recommended maximum limit is 6 pushes per minute per repository." Reads: "The recommended maximum limit is 15 operations per second per repository." These are recommendations per repository, not enforced errors; exceeding them risks "degraded repository health ... slow response times for basic Git operations and UI latency". Push size is enforced at 2 GB. Source: docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/repository-limits.
- Bitbucket Cloud: recommended under 2.0 GB; at 4.0 GB "you will only be able to push changes that undo the latest commits"; a Free workspace has "1GB of total repository storage within the workspace". Source: support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/reduce-repository-size/ (modified 2026-05-29).
- Claude Code: `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` is set in Bash and PowerShell tool subprocesses and hooks and "is updated on /clear"; `--resume <id>` keeps the resumed id; `--fork-session` makes a new id. Subagents share the parent id: observed on version 2.1.322, not documented. Source: code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars.md.
- Consequence for design v7: one push per write (or per claim) on one branch of one repository exceeds the GitHub push recommendation with a handful of active writers. 50 writers (requirement S3) would be far above it.

## Work tracker, design version 8 (family `git-budget`)

Base: design version 7 ("v7", record basicly-gtb19bg.60). Measured facts: verify/RESULTS.md.

Bad news first. Comments and fields reach others after p50 109 s, p95 218 s at 13 machines (measured). Five or more claims in one second can take over 10 s (measured: 9 of 13, maximum 26.5 s). Claims are not budgeted: 52 sessions that each claim every 8.7 minutes send 6 pushes per minute from claims alone (arithmetic). A 1,000,000-event project needs 0.5 to 0.7 GB (measured), so Bitbucket Free (1 GB per workspace, sourced) holds about one.

### 1. Decisions

#### 1.1 Owner decisions, each with a recommended answer

- **O1, What "shared in time" (N4) means.** Claim, take and unassign: settled within 10 s at p99 in steady state; an answer always within 30 s. Other events: within the bulk interval T times 1.2, so 72 s up to 4 active machines, 234 s at 13 (measured p95 218 s), 360 s at 20. The simulation shared on a timer, so the measurement is a best case. S6 (60 s for all events) is not met.
- **O2, Identity binding (X2).** Stays deferred; SSH signing prompted on Linux (measured, verify-service C5). `fsck` reports a writer id that pushes under a new commit author.
- **O3, Erasure (X5).** Not built. Events carry a random person id; name and email live only in `person` events. Erasure is an owner-run history rewrite with an `erasure` audit stub; each clone refuses until `fsck --accept-rewrite <head> --erasure <stub-id>`.
- **O4, Forecast (V6) against the SPEC.md:741 non-goal.** Drop "estimate" from the non-goal: the binding board question "when will the work be done" (requirements-r1.md:28) needs it. It is computed at read time and stores nothing.
- **O5, Commit hook refuses a commit with no record id.** Yes. This reverses v7 sections 8 and 9. It checks only for an id or `Record: none`, never status.
- **O6, Approved slices.** Slices S2, S3 and S4 change (section 12) and need new approval.

#### 1.2 Where the four designs disagree

- **Order**: `ord` stamped in each line (portable-core), not first-parent order (the other three). A reader with only the files, for example an export, then rebuilds claim order (section 2.4), and a later sequencer can write the same format with no migration.
- **Integrity**: one global chain of batch seals, not a chain per file (first-principles), because it also proves `ord`.
- **Registry**: an event log in vault format (evolve-v7, portable-core), not TOML files (git-native): one format, one conflict rule.
- **Vault scope**: one per project, not one per audience (portable-core), because the push budget is per repository.
- **Push at once**: claim, take, unassign, handover, project register. Not close, create or edge (git-native): they need no order.
- **Bulk rule**: the one rule that was simulated, `T = max(60 s, M × 60 / 4)`. The other three formulas are unmeasured.
- **Commit hook**: refuse a missing id, warn on an unheld record. Refusing an unheld record (evolve-v7) acts on stale state; warning only (portable-core) fails "never forget".
- **Misses and links**: stored events (evolve-v7, first-principles), so a lead without code clones sees them.
- **PR check**: no vault token (git-native); portable-core's token breaks X7.
- **Rotation**: by size, not by year (all four), because a busy writer's yearly file grows past the measured good case.

Dropped: stripe repositories, the HTTP sequencer adapter, a committed STATUS.md (0.8 to 1.9 KB per commit, measured).

### 2. Data

#### 2.1 Repositories

- **Registry**: one ordinary repository with the same files. Its events register projects, prefixes, aliases, archives, moves and code locations; it holds no titles or record ids. A hidden project uses its own registry.
- **Vault**: one ordinary repository per project, the unit of read access. Files: `vault.toml` (vault uid, format version, minimum tool version, budget constants), `FORMAT.md`, `reader.py`, `README.md` (what it is, how to read and delete it), `log/`.
- **Code repository**: `.basicly/tracker.toml` (registry URL, project uid, vault URL hint, prefixes) and one README line (C2).
- **Machine**: a mode-0700 user folder with one clone per vault and registry, named by uid; queue and caches live in its `.git`.

A person creates each empty repository on the forge. The tool calls no forge API and needs no token (X7).

#### 2.2 Ids

- Registry, vault, project and writer ids: random 128-bit; none contains a host (P2, P4).
- Writer id: one per clone (v7 section 3). Holder: (writer id, session id). Session id: `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, or an id from `basicly tracker session new` (D3).
- Event id: writer id plus 128 random bits, fixed at queue time. `link` and `miss` ids are `sha256(project, commit, record, kind)`, so observers agree.
- Record id: `<prefix>-<root>.<n>` (SPEC.md section 9.4). The registry gives each prefix one project; a rename adds an alias and the old prefix stays owned (P3).

#### 2.3 Files and rotation

Layout: `log/<writer-id>/<nnnnn>.jsonl`. The first line of each segment is the writer header. A writer opens a new segment at 1.5 MB. Nothing rewrites a file.

Why 1.5 MB: files that grew to 1.39 MB cost 640 B per event after a normal repack; files that grew to about 7.3 MB cost 3.3 KB (measured, verify/storage/p100k.log, d20k.log).

File count: 1,000,000 events at 1.39 KB raw (measured, before `ord` and seals) is 1.39 GB, so about 930 full segments plus one open segment per writer. That is under 1,000 at 50 writers by arithmetic only; the storage test (section 11) decides.

#### 2.4 Event format, version 1

One UTF-8 JSON object per LF line:

```text
{"v":1,"ord":8812,"id":"…","ts":"2026-11-11T09:00:00Z","project":"…","record":"abc-k3x9.2",
 "kind":"claim","writer":"…","session":"…","actor":{"kind":"agent","person":"…"},"data":{}}
```

- Every release reads every earlier `v` (L1). `ts` is UTC RFC 3339, evidence only (L6). `actor` names the kind and the responsible person (D4).
- Unknown kinds and fields are kept and skipped (SPEC.md section 4.5). Configuration is events, so an old event keeps the meaning it had at its `ord` (P5).
- Each batch ends with a seal: `{"v":1,"kind":"seal","ord":[a,b],"prev":…,"hash":sha256(prev + batch bytes),"tool":"<version>"}`. The first `prev` is `sha256(vault uid)`.
- Valid seals, from the files alone: start at the seal with the highest `ord` end (ties: lowest `hash`) and walk `prev` back to the first seal. Every other seal is void. A line counts only when a valid seal covers it. Under the tool, compare-and-swap pushes make the chain a straight line. A bypass merge makes a fork; the branch that later shares extend wins, and `fsck --repair` re-queues the other branch's events.

### 3. Write, share and read

#### 3.1 Write

A command redacts secrets and absolute paths (X4), appends the event to the clone queue under `LedgerLock`, and prints one line:

- `shared` when the push landed;
- `queued, shares within N s at the next tracker command or agent hook`, where N is the time to the next bulk slot. No daemon runs.

#### 3.2 Share

Under the share lock (v7 section 5):

1. Fetch. If the last seen tip is not an ancestor of the head, refuse and name `fsck --repair`.
2. Drop queued events whose ids are on the head.
3. Read H, the highest valid `ord`, and the last valid seal.
4. Stamp the queued events H+1 to H+k, append them and a seal to this writer's open segment, and build one commit with the head as its only parent.
5. Push plainly. On refusal, discard the stamps and go to step 1.
6. On success, record the last seen tip and remove the shared events from the queue. The v7 drain bound stays.

#### 3.3 Push budget

- **Urgent events**: claim, take, unassign, handover, project register. They push at once and carry every queued event.
- **Bulk events**: all others. They ride on any urgent push. Otherwise the clone shares every `T = max(60 s, M × 60 / 4)` seconds, times a random factor 0.8 to 1.2. M is the number of writers with a commit on the head in the last hour. The constants live in `vault.toml`.

This is the simulated rule (verify/contention/sim.py:144-146). With 52 sessions on 13 machines it gave 5.06 push attempts per minute and claim p99 6.3 s (measured).

A due share runs at every tracker command, agent hook, code pre-push hook, and every 30 s while the board is open.

Bursts: one clone per machine puts all its sessions' claims into one push. Nothing more is promised for 5 or more claims in the same second.

#### 3.4 Claim protocol

`basicly tracker claim <id>`:

1. Validate the id and the session id. No session id: exit 1.
2. Fetch and fold. Held by this session: exit 7. Held by another: exit 3, with no push.
3. `git ls-remote`, 5 s deadline. No answer: exit 5; nothing is queued.
4. Append the claim to the queue under `LedgerLock`.
5. Share (section 3.2) until a 30 s deadline. Another session on this machine may push the claim instead; that counts the same.
6. When the claim's id is on the fetched head, fold. Valid: exit 0. Void (another claim came first, also one in the same batch): exit 3.
7. Deadline: exit 4, "unsettled: claim queued; do not start work; run basicly tracker claim <id> --wait".

Exit codes for every command: 0 done; 1 refused, with the next command; 2 usage (argparse); 3 held by another session, with name, age and `--take`; 4 unsettled; 5 offline; 6 internal error, no traceback; 7 already held by this session.

After exit 4 the claim stays queued, and the next command or agent hook on this machine retries it. Local views show "unsettled (yours)"; other machines see nothing until it lands.

`--take` is valid, logged and names the old holder. `unassign` is valid only from the holder or with `--take` (fixes basicly-qtmesvv). `handover <id> --to <holder>` passes a claim. `resume <old-session>` takes back that session's claims after `/clear`. It is logged, names the old session, and is valid only from the same writer id (D2).

#### 3.5 Read

A read fetches when the last fetch is older than 20 s, folds new commits by `ord`, and applies the v7 holder verdicts: the first valid claim by `ord` wins. Every view prints freshness: last fetch age, last shared event per writer, queued count (V5). Offline, a read uses the last fetched state and prints its age (D6). All worktrees on a machine read one clone and queue (D1). Load: 13 clones at one fetch per 20 s give 0.65 reads per second; GitHub recommends at most 15 (sourced).

### 4. Many projects

- **Register**: `basicly tracker project add --name N --prefix P --vault <url> --code <url>` initializes the empty vault and pushes `project-register` at once. The first registration of a prefix by `ord` wins; a later one is refused by name with the owner (P1). `project list` shows all.
- **Isolation**: `project add` runs an anonymous `git ls-remote` on both URLs and refuses a vault that answers anonymously while the code repository does not (X1). Assumed until its real-host test passes.
- **Archive**: `project archive` makes vault writes refuse by name; `project restore` reverses it.
- **Portfolio**: the fold of every vault this machine can clone; a vault with no access shows "no access".
- **Dependencies**: an edge stores the full target id and resolves through the registry. Without access the target shows "hidden record".

### 5. Never forget

Code never changes a status. Each point refuses a missing link or reports it.

- **Commit-msg hook** (installed by `attach`, version-marked). Catches a commit with no record id and no `Record: none`. It auto-fills ` (<id>)` when the session holds exactly one claim. It warns, with the claim command, when the named record is not held (V4). Offline it passes and records a local miss. Cannot catch: `--no-verify`, a machine without `attach`, commits made on the forge.
- **Agent hooks** (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop). Show held, stale and unsettled claims, suggestions and queued events, and run a due share. Cannot catch: a person with no agent.
- **PR check** (CI template, no token). Catches a PR whose title and commits name no known prefix id or `none`, and a changed project uid. Cannot catch anything where it is not a required check (required checks need GitHub paid plans or public repositories, or Bitbucket Premium; v7 section 9).
- **Session start and every read** (`fsck --code`). Show suggestions from `closes <id>` and reverts (v7 section 8), merged commits with no record, in-progress records with no code activity, and stale claims. Store `link` and `miss` events (V3, L5). Cannot catch anything until an attached clone fetches the code default branch.

What slips past, and how it still shows: a bypassed commit becomes a `miss` at the next audit; a quiet session shows an old "last shared" time; an unsettled claim elsewhere is invisible until it lands.

### 6. Visibility

- **Portfolio** (`basicly tracker portfolio`, board): per project, holders, blocked, stale claims, ready count, closed in 7 days, misses, forecast, freshness (V1).
- **Stale claims**: no event or linked commit by the holder for 2 hours (agent session) or 3 days (person), both configurable and assumed. Flagged with holder and age, never released. `claim <id> --take` names the old holder (V2).
- **Forecast**: a range from closed events per week, with sample size (after O4).
- **Resume after /clear**: SessionStart lists claims of other sessions on this writer, with the age of their last event, and prints `basicly tracker resume <old-session>`. The tool cannot know that a session ended; the person or agent decides.
- **Output**: versioned `--json`; no prompt, editor or pager (D5, D7).

### 7. Security

- **Credentials**: only the user's git credentials, with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`; no token is written (X7).
- **Input**: `git_runner.py` validates ids and URLs (only `https`, `ssh`); hooks get paths through environment variables.
- **Untrusted text**: record text reaches an agent only between `<<<record-text` and `record-text>>>`, control characters stripped; nothing runs or follows it (X6).
- **Tamper detection**: the rewrite check, the seal chain (a changed or removed line of any writer, also in an export) and the writer header. Every clone reports at its next command (X3).
- **Redaction**: on by default on every write path (section 3.1, X4).
- **Board**: loopback only; a state change needs a per-session token and matching Host and Origin (X8).

### 8. Longevity

- **FORMAT.md** in every repository: line format, seals, holder verdicts, fold.
- **reader.py**: standard library, at most 300 lines; CI checks it folds to the kit's records (L2).
- **Export**: `basicly tracker export <dir>` writes the log by `ord`, `FORMAT.md`, `reader.py` and a SHA-256 manifest; `import <dir>` restores and checks seals (L4). Recovery point: each writer's last share.
- **Host move**: `basicly tracker move <new-url>` pushes all history to an empty target and appends `vault-moved` to vault and registry. No id changes (P4).
- **Archive**: `project archive` (section 4); the vault stays readable.
- **Growth budget**: 0.64 KB per event (measured, normal repack). Assumed load: 20,000 events per project per year, so 10 years is about 130 MB. Clone of 100,000 events: 1.5 s locally (measured). `status` warns at 70 % of the host limit; `vault continue <new-url>` starts a successor vault and the fold reads both.

### 9. Install, upgrade, migration, removal

- **Install**: one README line, `uv tool install` from the basicly GitHub repository at a pinned tag (A7), then `basicly tracker attach`. Each missing piece is refused with its exact command (A3).
- **Mixed versions**: each seal records the tool version. An old tool reads what it can and refuses a write below the minimum in `vault.toml`, naming the upgrade command (A1).
- **Upgrade**: `uv tool upgrade basicly-tracker`, then `basicly tracker upgrade`: state and hooks, both versions printed, resumable, downgrade refused (A2). `upgrade --vault` raises the minimum only after every writer active in 30 days sealed with the new version.
- **Migration**: the in-repository ledger uses v7 section 11 (freeze, import, verify, cutover PR); the import stamps `ord` in today's fold order and keeps ids. `migrate --from beads|beans <path> --preview` imports with count and digest checks (A5).
- **Removal**: v7 section 13 per project; `basicly tracker uninstall` per machine exports the queue, removes everything, lists leftovers (A4).
- **Platforms**: standard library only. CI runs install, attach, claim, serve and removal on Linux, macOS and Windows, in a path with spaces (A6).

### 10. Recovery

Commands omit `basicly tracker`.

- Crash during a share: queue intact, ids dedupe. `share`.
- Torn queue tail: cut back automatically.
- Host outage: claims exit 5, other events queue. `share`.
- Force-push or rewrite: shares refuse. `fsck --repair`.
- Push by plain git: unsealed lines are void and reported. `fsck --repair` re-queues this writer's lines.
- Lost machine: unshared events are lost; its claims go stale. `claim <id> --take`.
- Stale claim: flagged, never released. `claim <id> --take`, which names the old holder.
- Vault lost on the host: any clone or export holds the history up to its last fetch. `move <new-url>` from that clone, or `import <dir>`.
- Unsettled claim: queued and shown. `claim <id> --wait`.
- Prefix race: the later registration is void. `project add` with another prefix.
- Half-done migration: resumes by event id. `migrate --to-backlog`, then `migrate --verify`.
- Corrupt clone: the queue file survives. `reclone`.
- Vault near its size limit: a warning. `vault continue <new-url>`.
- Crash during upgrade or move: run `upgrade` or `move <new-url>` again.

### 11. Proof tests

Local CI on bare repositories with injected latency. "Real host" means sandbox GitHub and Bitbucket repositories, which need owner approval.

- N1: 1,000 tracker writes leave the code repository clean. Real host: two code PRs stay mergeable.
- N2: 8 processes in 3 worktrees, 1,000 events: each lands once, also after kills.
- N3: A `closes <id>` squash gives one suggestion; a `--no-verify` commit, an admin merge and a direct push each give one `miss` on another machine.
- N4 exclusivity: 3 clones, and 8 sessions in one clone, claim one record; exactly one gets exit 0, the rest exit 3.
- N4, S4: 52 sessions on 13 machines: claim p99 at most 10 s, all answered within 30 s. Real host: half a day.
- N4 bulk, S5: same rig: bulk p95 within the printed N plus 30 s; at most 6 push attempts per minute on average. Real host: latency against an idle baseline.
- Order: delete `.git` and rebuild from the files: same holders. A `pull --rebase` push of unsealed lines and a bypass merge fork are each void and reported.
- S1, L3: 1,000,000 events, 1.5 MB cap: at most 0.7 GB after a normal repack, under 1,000 files.
- S2: 10,000 records, 4 cores, Linux and Windows: read p95 1 s, append p95 200 ms.
- S8 clone: 10-year vault clones within 60 s at 10 Mbit/s.
- X1 probe: Real host: four repositories; anonymous `ls-remote` answers right, no prompt, no hang.
- D3, real host: a session and its subagent see one `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`.
- A1: Versions n and n+1 write one vault; nothing lost; the old one refuses by name.
- L2: `reader.py` and the kit give equal digests.

### 12. Build slices

In this section S1 to S11 name slices; elsewhere S1 to S8 name section 6 requirements.

Slices S2 to S4 need new approval (O6).

- S2 fold and holder verdicts: order by `ord` and valid seals; adds `v`.
- S3 attach, queue, share, read: uid clones, project uid, segments, `ord`, seals, bulk interval. The 52-session test passes before merge.
- S4 claims: exit codes, pre-check, 30 s deadline, unsettled state, take, handover, resume.
- S8 registry (new): `project` commands, portfolio, isolation probe.
- S5 audit: adds stored `link` and `miss` events.
- S6 hooks and PR check: commit-msg id rule, agent hooks, PR check with no token.
- S9 longevity (new): FORMAT.md, reader.py, export, import, move, vault continue.
- S7 migration: v7 section 11 plus beads and beans.
- S10 lifecycle (new): upgrade, doctor, uninstall, three-platform CI.
- S11 forecast (new): after O4.

Build in the order listed. Reused: slice S1 (`git_runner.py`, built), `LedgerLock`, `events.py`, `holders.py`, `fsck.py`, `migrate.py`, `beads.py`, `beans.py`, `board.py`.

### 13. Section 6 requirements not met

- S4: not met for 5 or more claims in the same second.
- S5: met as a mean only. The busiest minute reaches 12 to 18, and claims are not budgeted.
- S6: not met for bulk events above 4 active machines. GitHub's push guidance wins.
- S7: queued events share at the next command after the network returns.
- S1: the file limit holds to about 1,000,000 events. Bitbucket Free holds about one such project.
- X1: partly. Registry readers see project names; a hidden project uses its own registry. The probe is unverified.
- X2, X5, V6: owner decisions O2, O3, O4.
- X9: roles are forge permissions per vault.
- V7: notices without polling need a server.
- D3: partly. Codex, Copilot and persons run `session new`.

Every other section 6 id is met by sections 2 to 9 and stays unproven until section 11 runs.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a session root whose candidate lanes are not dispatchable when basicly loop preflight runs then it reports each candidates band verdict and working-set size and names the ones with no parseable scope instead of only the aggregate fallback forecast
payload.description:
## Context

`basicly loop preflight <root>` answers "what would a pass cost" in aggregate only. Twice in one
session (2026-08-01) the operator had to hand-write a python query against
`decompose.resolve_dispatch_sizing` to answer the question that actually decides a run: **which
candidate lanes would the band admit, and at what size**.

`supervise.band_coverage` already produces exactly this report, but preflight reaches it only via
`_print_preflight_spend`'s `if lanes:` branch — i.e. only when lanes are *already dispatchable*.
With a halted grant, or any root whose children are not yet ready, `lanes` is empty and preflight
prints just the fallback line:

```
per-lane:  16002352 tokens assumed for an unsizeable lane (measured)
forecast:  ~80011760 tokens if all 5 lanes start (cap x per-lane)
```

That 80M is the fallback assumption multiplied by the concurrency cap. It is not a measurement, and
it reads exactly like one. Measured on this repo's own tracker the same moment, over the 16 open
`basicly-jr0l` children: 1 lane in band, 1 below `working_set_min`, 3 above `working_set_max`, and
11 with no parseable scope. A grant minted against the 80M line would be minted against a number
describing none of that.

This is the same class of failure as basicly-jr0l.60 and basicly-tuy6: the information exists, the
gate computes it, and nothing surfaces it to the person deciding. Preflight is the documented
pre-run command (`basicly loop preflight` is what the operating notes say to run instead of
recalling a checklist), so it is the right place.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a session root whose candidate lanes are not dispatchable when `basicly loop preflight` runs then it reports each candidate's band verdict and working-set size, and names the ones with no parseable scope, instead of only the aggregate fallback forecast

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_cli_loop.py`

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-5p49` shipped the tree-growth signal and met four of its five acceptance criteria. This bead is the fifth.

The signal prints from `basicly verify`. It is not recorded on the run and it does not appear in the supervised pass line, so it is visible to whoever runs a gate and invisible to whoever reads a pass afterwards.

## Why the lane stopped rather than reaching

Two reasons, both stated by the implementer rather than discovered later.

The scope globs on `basicly-5p49` were `.scripts/`, `basicly.toml` and `tests/`. The pass line comes from `supervise._report_coverage`, beside the existing band and spend lines, and the run fields come from `run_record`. Both are outside those globs.

And there is a hard blocker. `src/basicly/supervise.py` is frozen by the module-size ratchet and may only shrink, so adding a report line to it fails the gate today. That is the same shape `basicly-r343` hit: a ratchet refuses a change to a file, and the real fix is a split that has nothing to do with the change.

## What that makes this bead depend on

`basicly-wotk` extracts the outcome routing sink out of `supervise.py` and is the item that gives that file headroom. Doing this one first means either a second waiver or a refactor bolted onto a reporting change.

## Why it is worth doing at all

The standing rule is that a demoted or advisory number must still be recorded on the run, surfaced in the pass line and kept falsifiable against the ledger. A signal that only prints during a gate run satisfies none of those. It also cannot earn the right to block, because earning it requires a firing history and nothing records one.

## Acceptance

- When a supervised pass completes, then its line states the tree-growth value and the window it covers, beside the existing band and spend lines.
- When a run record is written, then it carries the same value and window.
- When the value is read back from the ledger, then it is comparable across passes, so a trend is computable without re-running the gate.
- When the signal has no window to measure, for example in a shallow clone, then the pass line says so rather than printing a zero.
- When any of this is added, then `supervise.py` does not grow past its frozen baseline.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/run_record.py`
- `.scripts/check_tree_growth.py`
- `tests/`

## Depends on

`basicly-wotk`, which gives `supervise.py` the headroom this needs.

## Demonstration

Run a supervised pass and read the tree-growth line beside the band line, then read the same value back out of the run record.

payload.description:
Retro finding (v0.5.0 and v0.5.1 this session): the release changelog generator produces the new section in the wrong place and with a lint violation, so it needs hand-fixing every release.

Root cause: .scripts/generate_release_changelog.py _insert_index returns the index of the first "## " heading, which is "## [Unreleased]". The new "## vX.Y.Z" section is therefore inserted ABOVE [Unreleased] instead of below it, and the join leaves two consecutive blank lines before the following section (markdownlint MD012). Both releases this session required a manual reorder plus a blank-line fix.

Proposed fix: insert the new release section immediately AFTER an existing "## [Unreleased]" section (keeping [Unreleased] on top), and never emit a double blank line at the seam. Fall back sensibly (insert after the intro) when no [Unreleased] section exists.

## Acceptance Criteria

- generate_release_changelog.py inserts a new "## vX.Y.Z - DATE" section immediately after an existing "## [Unreleased]" section so [Unreleased] stays at the top; when none exists it inserts after the header intro.
- The output has no consecutive blank lines at the insertion seam (markdownlint MD012 passes on the generated CHANGELOG.md without hand-editing).
- A regression test covers insertion order with an [Unreleased] section present and asserts no double blank lines.
- Once correct, trim the "reordering/curation" caveat in the release-process skill to only the genuine curation step (grouping raw commits into Added/Fixed).

payload.description:
## Context
Earlier native comment commands queued raw kind=comment wrappers. Vault carried reads and export consume ledger wrappers, so those old comments are not represented as ordinary ledger notes. The current vault goal starts from an empty private vault and new C2 comments are carried ledger notes. Orchestrator deferred legacy projection from this critical path on 2026-11-13; no known kept goal vault requires raw native comments. Codex-1 requested one common projection for rich read and export before such a vault is retained.
## Proposed design
Validate the raw record, text and public native identity. Derive a stable valid note id using a payload origin pointer to that public native wrapper id; distinct raw ids with duplicate text stay distinct. Preserve existing ledger-wrapper ids and payloads exactly and never rewrite vault history. Use the same projection in read and export, including own pending visibility. Until then, the shared read seam explicitly reports the number of legacy comments it cannot show and names this backlog record.
## Scope
Only vaults with retained legacy native comments need this follow-up. It does not block the fresh vault tracker and workspace cutover. Coordinate the narrow view/export delegation with their owner; no private id map is required.

payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-09-07, after reading a record page that showed a title and no body: *"how should i then use this to drive test-driven development to write tests first and make them pass later? ... I as human, if that was my backlog i wouldnt even know where to start."*

And the standard they set: *"you can follow the INVEST criteria and benchmark against them every time you write a record (story, task). Also Jeffries C3 for writing stories can also help. I am demanding this because to me it looks like content of the records is not independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable - thus it is hard to implement."*

## Measured

Folded from the ledger on 2026-09-07 over the 304 records `units[]` lists, with a positive control on `basicly-lc2bd3v.7` run before the zero was believed:

| active records | 304 |
| --- | --- |
| with a `## Acceptance Criteria` section | 196 (64%) |
| a body but no criteria | 99 |
| no body at all | 9 |

So **108 records can be dispatched with nothing to verify the result against**. `basicly-e2mz.38` filed this at *fifty five*; it has doubled since, which is what says guidance did not hold it.

## Why a gate and not a checklist

`basicly-lc2bd3v.8` established the pattern one surface over: a requirement restated in four sessions and fixed site by site is a requirement no review is holding. The plan gate already checks acceptance criteria for a *decomposed child* - `plan_gate.missing_fields` tests `bool(acceptance)` - and a record created straight from the terminal never passes through it. That is the hole.

## The owner's chosen strength

Gate at dispatch, advise everywhere else. A record may be captured from a terminal in one line; that is how the owner builds the backlog and it must stay cheap. It may not *enter BUILD* without something a test can be written from.

## What is checkable and what is judgement

Checkable, so it gates: **Testable** - an acceptance section with at least one criterion; **Valuable** - a context naming who wants it and why; **Small** - a token budget; **Independent** - dependencies declared or explicitly none. Judgement, so it advises only: **Negotiable** and **Estimable**.

Jeffries' three Cs map onto sections the format already has. Card is the title, Conversation is Context, Confirmation is Acceptance Criteria. A record missing Confirmation is the population measured above.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a record is dispatched to BUILD, THE ENGINE SHALL refuse it where it carries no acceptance criteria, and the refusal SHALL name the missing section rather than reporting the record invalid.
- WHERE a record is created or updated outside dispatch, THE ENGINE SHALL record the same finding as advisory and SHALL NOT refuse the write.
- A REPORT SHALL name every active record failing a checkable INVEST condition, grouped by condition, so the 108 are a worked backlog rather than a number.
- THE REPORT SHALL run a positive control, so a zero distinguishes an empty population from a probe that found nothing.
- THE JUDGEMENT CONDITIONS, negotiable and estimable, SHALL NOT gate, and the report SHALL say so where it names them.
- A TEST SHALL drive a record with no criteria at dispatch and assert the refusal names the missing section.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/plan_entry.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `.scripts/check_record_invest.py`
- `tests/test_record_invest.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.added.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `110000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: run the report and read the 108 by name, then dispatch a record with no criteria and read the refusal

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## Context

When a record reaches BUILD carrying nothing a test can be written from, the lane has to invent the requirement it is verifying against, so I want the engine to refuse that dispatch and to name every record already in that state, so I can drive the backlog test-first instead of guessing what each record meant.

Owner, 2026-09-07, after reading a record page that showed a title and no body: *"how should i then use this to drive test-driven development to write tests first and make them pass later? ... I as human, if that was my backlog i wouldnt even know where to start."* And the standard: *"you can follow the INVEST criteria and benchmark against them every time you write a record (story, task). Also Jeffries C3 for writing stories can also help."*

Owner, 2026-09-08, refining the Valuable condition: *"because valuable entails a persona that wants it, which sometimes we do not have, instead of using the user story voice, use job story voice ... one should never force a persona in the story that does not need it or have it. for example a story about patching the system may be causes by a situation, which is publishing of vulnerabilities, and does not involve a person."*

The owner asks for two separable things, and the engine holds one of them:

| the owner asks for | the phase that reads it | enforced before this record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| acceptance criteria, to verify against and write tests from | VERIFY | yes, `policy.definition_of_ready` |
| a requirement, to validate against | VALIDATE | no section holds one |

## Corrected measurement

The first filing of this record claimed **108** records carry nothing to verify against. That figure is wrong and this record supersedes it. It counted the `## Acceptance Criteria` body heading by substring and ignored the structured `acceptance_criteria` field, which `policy._has_acceptance_criteria` documents as an equally valid carrier. 82 active records carry their criteria in that field alone and were all counted as missing. The fault is the one `basicly-lc2bd3v.8` also turned on: a filter on one carrier hides a population.

Re-derived 2026-09-08 over `tracker.all_records`, with the carriers read by the engine's own `plan_record.section_entries` and the field test from `policy._has_acceptance_criteria`:

| carrier | active records |
| --- | --- |
| body section only | 151 |
| structured field only | 82 |
| both | 37 |
| **neither** | **36** |
| total active | 306 |

Two further defects the count exposed:

- **6 records carry the heading and zero parsed criteria**, so a bare heading clears the gate having stated nothing: `basicly-c0k6a4`, `basicly-cs5k8y`, `basicly-jr0l.56`, `basicly-u2hl.60`, `basicly-u2hl.61`, `basicly-vkh0.42.12`. `plan_record` already documents this lenient edge in prose; it is live in the tracker.
- **The 36 are concentrated, not 36 authoring lapses.** `basicly-a4q3` contributes 10 and `basicly-u2hl` 7, so 17 of 36 come from two decomposes that emitted children with no criteria. A gate at dispatch alone would refuse them one at a time; the report is what makes them a worked backlog.

## What is already built, and what is not

Established by reading the code on 2026-09-08, with a positive control run before any zero was believed (`basicly-0bj8q1` reads `ready=True`, `basicly-0u7uns` reads `ready=False, missing=('## Steps to Reproduce', '## Acceptance Criteria')`):

| the first filing's criterion | state |
| --- | --- |
| refuse a dispatch to BUILD with no acceptance criteria, naming the section | **already built** — `policy.definition_of_ready` requires them of every type, and `loop._on_classify` runs it before `_start_build_leaf` |
| record the same finding as advisory outside dispatch | not built — no DoR call on the record-write path |
| a report naming every record failing a checkable condition | not built — `basicly policy dor` takes one id and has no sweep |
| the report runs a positive control | not built |
| negotiable and estimable never gate | holds, because nothing gates them |

So the refusal is not the work. The work is the requirement carrier, the two parsing defects, and the report.

## The Valuable condition, in the owner's voice rule

Bill Wake's original INVEST defines Valuable as *"it needs to be valuable to the customer"*. It requires no persona and no named role. The first filing of this record glossed Valuable as *"a context naming who wants it and why"*, which is stricter than INVEST and is the over-specification the owner's 2026-09-08 instruction removes.

Valuable is therefore satisfied by a stated **trigger**, in either voice:

| voice | shape | triggered by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| job story | `When <situation>, I want to <motivation>, so I can <outcome>.` | a situation |
| user story | `As a <persona>, I want <goal>, so that <benefit>.` | a persona |

A record may carry both. Mike Cohn: *"The two techniques are quite compatible and there's no reason to view them as mutually exclusive."* A record must never be refused for omitting a persona, and a checker must not pattern-match the persona shape alone, because that teaches an author to prepend a fabricated `As a developer` to a story that has no person in it. Cohn names that failure directly: *"When a large set of user stories all begin with 'As a user...' you've got a set of stories for whom the user is not very important."* The patching case the owner gives is the test: the trigger is the publication of a vulnerability and no person appears.

Jeffries' three Cs map onto the sections: Card is the title, Conversation is the trigger, Confirmation is the acceptance criteria.

Sources, verified 2026-09-08: Wake, *INVEST in Good Stories, and SMART Tasks* (xp123.com); Cohn, *Job Stories: A Viable Alternative to User Stories* (mountaingoatsoftware.com); Klement, *Replacing The User Story With The Job Story* — not readable, HTTP 403, so his position against coexistence is recorded from secondary description only. That disagreement does not reach the gate, because a checker accepting either voice satisfies both authors.

## What gates and what advises

The owner's chosen strength: gate at dispatch, advise everywhere else. A record must stay capturable from a terminal in one line, because that is how the backlog is built. It may not enter BUILD without a trigger and a criterion.

| condition | checkable as | gate or advice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Testable | at least one criterion that parses, in either carrier | gate at dispatch |
| Valuable | a trigger section holding either voice's shape | gate at dispatch |
| Small | a token budget | gate at dispatch |
| Independent | dependencies declared, or explicitly none | gate at dispatch |
| a generic persona carrying nothing | the `As a user` string | advice only |
| the situation is a real situation | judgement | advice only |
| Negotiable, Estimable | judgement | advice only, and the report says so |

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a record is dispatched to BUILD, THE ENGINE SHALL refuse it where it carries no trigger, and the refusal SHALL name the trigger section and print both accepted voices so an author picks one rather than defaulting to the persona.
- THE ENGINE SHALL accept a job story trigger with no persona anywhere in the record, and SHALL NOT refuse a record for omitting a persona.
- WHERE the acceptance criteria section carries a heading and no criterion that parses, THE ENGINE SHALL treat the record as carrying none, so a bare heading no longer clears the gate.
- THE ENGINE SHALL read both acceptance carriers, the body section and the structured field, and a criterion in either SHALL satisfy Testable.
- WHERE a record is created or updated outside dispatch, THE ENGINE SHALL record every failing condition as advisory and SHALL NOT refuse the write.
- A REPORT SHALL name every active record failing a checkable condition, grouped by condition, and SHALL group a family's children under their root so a concentrated decompose reads as one cause.
- THE REPORT SHALL run a positive control, so a zero distinguishes an empty population from a probe that found nothing.
- THE REPORT SHALL state that negotiable and estimable are judgement conditions that do not gate, where it names them.
- A TEST SHALL drive the owner's patching case — a job story trigger naming a published vulnerability, with no person in it — and assert the dispatch is allowed.
- A TEST SHALL drive a record whose trigger is absent and assert the refusal names the trigger section and both voices.
- A TEST SHALL drive a record carrying a bare acceptance heading and assert the refusal, so the lenient edge is closed by a regression rather than by prose.
- A TEST SHALL assert the report's count against the 36 measured here, so a later drift in either carrier reader fails.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/plan_record.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `.scripts/check_record_invest.py`
- `tests/test_record_invest.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
- `changelog.d/basicly-q1ve1fn.added.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `140000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: run the report and read the 36 by name, dispatch a record with no trigger and read the refusal naming both voices, then dispatch the patching job story with no persona and watch it pass

payload.text:
[decision 2026-09-08] The trigger gate applies to EVERY work type, with no exemption.

Owner, asked whether to exempt bug and chore: *"i said apply to all issue types, becaue if we only apply to so called value bearing ones, there is a danger that agents will crate the ones that do not need it just to quicker pass the gate"*

The exemption I had recommended keyed on `issue_type`, and `issue_type` is chosen by the same agent the gate is meant to bind. So the exemption is an escape hatch the gated party controls: an agent facing a trigger it cannot write reclassifies the record as a `chore` and the gate lets it through. The cost of the wider gate is real and measured - 305 of 306 active records carry no trigger in either voice and each needs one written before it can build - but a gate with a self-declared exemption measures nothing at all.

The general rule this is an instance of: never key a gate's exemption on a field the gated party writes. It is the same fault as binding a ratchet on a marker whose absence is ambiguous.

Rejected alternatives, both measured before the choice:
- exempt bug and chore, gating feature/task/epic only: 208 records in scope, 97 exempt. Refused for the reason above.
- gate the section heading and advise the shape: 83 records refused instead of 305. Refused because 223 records already carry a Context heading filled with prose, which is the state that opened this record.

payload.description:
WHY: basicly currently authors a skill as .basicly/core/skills/<name>/skill.yaml (fields: name, description, instructions, technologies) and renders ONLY a single SKILL.md via skills.py:render_skill_md/sync_skills. It does NOT copy references/, scripts/, assets/, or any additional files to the skill roots. The Agent Skills spec (https://agentskills.io/specification) allows a skill directory to contain SKILL.md (required) plus scripts/, references/, assets/, and '... Any additional files or directories'. To author powerful skills (e.g. a python skill with a long references/ style guide + a fixer scripts/), the engine must project the whole skill directory.

SCOPE / FILES:
- src/basicly/skills.py: sync_skills / check_synced_skills / discover_skills / render_skill_md — copy every file & subdirectory of the source skill dir (except the skill.yaml source, which renders to SKILL.md) into each destination root (.claude/skills/<name>/ and .agents/skills/<name>/), verbatim, preserving structure. Prune on technology deselection. Add/verify freshness in check.
- src/basicly/schema.py + .basicly/core/schemas/skill.schema.json: extend the skill source to support the spec's optional frontmatter passthrough — license, compatibility, metadata (map), allowed-tools — rendered into SKILL.md frontmatter. Keep 'technologies' (basicly-internal scoping; NOT emitted into SKILL.md frontmatter, or emitted under metadata — decide and document).
- Generated-marker / protect-generated hooks (.basicly/core/hooks/protect-generated*.py): SKILL.md stays generated (marker), but bundled reference/script/asset files are HAND-AUTHORED sources that must be copied but NOT carry the generated marker and NOT be clobbered/pruned wrongly. Define the rule and enforce it.
- .basicly/generated-manifest.json: track projected skill files (including copied resources) so build/check/uninstall stay consistent.
- catalog-lint (.basicly/core/hooks/catalog-lint.py + src/basicly/catalog_lint.py): validate skill dirs against the spec — name matches dir (1-64 chars, lowercase a-z0-9 and single hyphens, no leading/trailing/consecutive hyphen), description non-empty <=1024 chars, SKILL.md body kept small (warn > ~500 lines per spec progressive disclosure), file references one level deep.
- basicly build / skills-build / skills-check / install / uninstall: end-to-end still green with resource files present.
- docs/architecture.md: document the full-spec skill layout and the source->projection mapping.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. A skill authored as .basicly/core/skills/<name>/ with skill.yaml + references/REF.md + scripts/x.sh + assets/y + an arbitrary extra file/dir projects ALL of them (unchanged bytes) into BOTH .claude/skills/<name>/ and .agents/skills/<name>/, alongside the rendered SKILL.md.
2. Optional frontmatter (license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools) round-trips from skill.yaml into SKILL.md frontmatter per spec; omitting them yields today's minimal frontmatter.
3. Technology deselection prunes the whole projected skill dir (all resources), not just SKILL.md.
4. basicly check / skills-check --all-default-roots / hooks-check / catalog lint all pass; protect-generated does not flag hand-authored resource files, and does not allow manual edits to generated SKILL.md.
5. New unit tests cover: full-dir copy, extra '...' files, frontmatter passthrough, prune-on-deselect, and check-detects-drift for a resource file.
6. 'skills-ref validate ./<projected-skill>' (https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills/tree/main/skills-ref) passes for a projected skill, or a documented reason if that tool is unavailable in-repo.

SPEC: https://agentskills.io/specification (directory structure incl. the '...' line; frontmatter table; progressive disclosure: metadata ~100 tokens, SKILL.md < ~5000 tokens / < 500 lines, resources on demand; file references one level deep; validation via skills-ref).

payload.description: Reproduced from a consumer canary: a repo with a 0.5.1-era .pre-commit-config.yaml runs basicly install on 0.12.0, install exits 0 printing repo converged, and beads-commit-msg-script survives pointing at .basicly/core/hooks/beads-commit-msg.py which 0.12.0 does not ship. Measured on basicly 0.21.5 (basicly-tracker 0.2.1) on 2026-10-09, in a beads (br) migration from a user install on WSL. The import damaged the notes of 6 records and redacted a literal C:\ example in a description.

Cause: beads.py rule windows-drive-path is [A-Za-z]:\\ plus a path tail. Notes that hold the two characters backslash-n after a colon, such as "provision_lefthook.py:\n1.", match it. A real line break does not match.

Reproduction (scratch ledger, basicly-tracker from tag v0.21.5):
1. Write a beads JSONL record with notes "see provision_lefthook.py:\\n1. PINNED_VERSION" (JSON-escaped, so the text holds a backslash and n).
2. basicly-tracker import <ledger> <export>; then show the record.
Observed: notes = "see provision_lefthook.p<redacted:windows-drive-path> PINNED_VERSION". The y, the backslash-n and "1." are gone.
3. A description "Use a literal C:\ path as an example." imports as "Use a literal <redacted:windows-drive-path> path as an example."
4. basicly-tracker update <ledger> <id> --field "description=see provision_lefthook.py:\n1. PINNED_VERSION and <redacted:windows-drive-path>" keeps the text unchanged, including <redacted:windows-drive-path>

Expected: one redaction rule for both write paths. The import keeps text that is not a real path, or flags a real path and keeps the text around it.
payload.title: Import redaction reads a literal backslash-n after a colon as a Windows drive path

payload.value:
When a beads import holds a drive letter inside a word followed by a backslash, such as py:\n1., the imported text shall be unchanged.
When a beads import holds a bare drive root with no path after it, the imported text shall be unchanged.
When text holds a real drive path such as <redacted:windows-drive-path>, every copy of the rule shall still redact it.
